talks.title: Modernizing Incident Response Using Techniques that Scale
talks.teaser: Discusses modernizing Incident Response Using Techniques that Scale and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The speakers, who run a small managed detection and response firm, argue that many incident response teams are slowed by bespoke scripts, dependence on a single commercial EDR, reliance on other departments for firewall changes, and habits such as full-disk imaging that can add days to an investigation. They frame speed as the key measure, since attackers now move within hours and dwell time keeps shrinking.

They propose triage acquisition in place of full disk images, collecting only the artifacts that matter, such as event logs, registry hives and prefetch files. Velociraptor handles collection across Windows, macOS and Linux, and labels applied in its interface can trigger automated collection. Hayabusa runs Sigma and its own detection logic over collected event logs to create retroactive detections, while Plaso builds super timelines from the artifacts. Timesketch lets a team annotate and analyze those timelines together, and OpenRelic chains these tools into containerized workflows, with optional LLM-assisted analysis.

The second speaker presented an open-source pipeline that connects Velociraptor, OpenRelic and Timesketch through a single install script and custom Velociraptor artifacts that watch for finished triage collections. A live demo collected event logs and produced a Hayabusa timeline in Timesketch within minutes, while Plaso processing ran longer on limited cores. The takeaway is to measure how long each phase of an investigation takes, prefer triage over full images, and reduce dependence on single products and other teams.

talks.title: Day 2
talks.teaser: Outlines day 2 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
This full-day recording from Security Fest 2025 covers the second day of the event, with sessions on retro hardware, privacy, network appliances, forensics and threat intelligence, followed by the closing ceremony. It opens with a Commodore 64 project that connects the computer to a small local language model through a user-port module. The builders explain the challenge rules, the hardware choices, and why they moved from fine-tuning a tiny model to a retrieval-augmented setup that answers from uploaded manuals. They also describe the power and cooling problems they hit along the way.

Later sessions cover a peer-to-peer app framework meant to keep communications private without central servers, with an overview of its onion-style routing, encrypted local storage and distributed data design. A research talk then examines a VPN appliance, showing how weak code hygiene, a path confusion issue in the web server and a predictable backup code generator combined into a remote compromise, which was reported to the vendor for patching. Another session walks through anti-forensics techniques attackers use on Windows and Linux, and how responders can still recover traces from the file table, journals and memory.

The final sessions cover incident response at scale, showing a triage collection and automated timeline pipeline built on open-source tools, and a threat intelligence talk on giving small teams useful intelligence through open sources, automation and a platform choice. The day closes with CTF and village awards and thanks to sponsors and volunteers. The main takeaway across the day is that defenders can close gaps by automating collection, validating what they find, and reviewing the weak points attackers rely on.
